planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil tops 70F, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early and transplant out.

directions: Bred for personal-size portions rather than a whole family, Honeypatch produces compact 5-6 inch fruit weighing under a pound on short 4-5 foot vines, making it a good fit for smaller gardens. Thin to one plant every 24 inches in fertile, well-drained soil and water on a schedule that lets the foliage dry fully between waterings to discourage disease. Protect young plants with row cover for an early growth boost, removing covers once flowers open so pollinators can reach them, and let fruit fully ripen on the vine for peak sweetness.

common_name: Kuroda Dawn Carrot (Yellow Carrot with Green Shoulders)

planting.note: Direct sow anytime from spring through about 10 weeks before a hard fall frost; this variety does not transplant well.

directions: This yellow-rooted carrot is distinguished by green shoulders that catch the light where the root pokes above the soil line, and it delivers a crisp, sweet bite without the earthiness typical of standard carrots. Sow thickly and thin to about 2 inches apart in deep, fertile, well-drained soil at pH 6.0-6.8 so roots can elongate to their full 6-8 inch length unobstructed. It stores well for months when kept cold, unwashed, and with tops removed, making it a good succession crop for continuous harvest.

planting.note: Start seed in plug trays indoors about 6 weeks ahead, then transplant 3-4 plants per plug at 6-inch spacing to keep shafts straight rather than curved.

directions: Ten years in the breeding of Hans Bongers, this allium merges leek sweetness with a mild hint of garlic in one mild-flavored shaft. Seedlings do best in cooler 60-70F conditions since warmer temperatures reduce germination, and crowding more than four seedlings per plug cell causes shafts to bend instead of growing straight. Harvest while shafts are still about half an inch across for the most tender texture, and watch for allium leaf miner, using exclusion netting if it is a problem in your area.

planting.note: Start seed on a heat mat 5-6 weeks before the last frost, then harden off and transplant after frost danger passes.

directions: A paste tomato developed at Oregon State University, this semi-determinate variety produces 3-4 inch deep purple-red fruit whose anthocyanin coloring intensifies with more direct sun exposure. Provide trellis or stake support and fertile, well-drained soil near pH 6.5, watering with drip irrigation to keep foliage dry and reduce disease pressure. Prune nearby foliage that shades the fruit if you want to maximize the purple color for sauces and roasting.

common_name: Beauregarde Snow Pea (Anthocyanin-Rich Purple Snow Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil reaches 45F, succession planting every two weeks until temperatures exceed 70F, or sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost for a second crop.

directions: Named for Violet Beauregarde and bred by Michael Mazourek, these snow peas carry high anthocyanin levels that give the pods a deep purple color that holds even after cooking. Sow thickly without thinning in well-drained soil between pH 6.0-7.0, and set up a trellis since the vines need about 4 feet of row spacing to climb properly. For the best flavor, let pods swell past the usual flat snow-pea stage until small peas are visible inside before harvesting, and watch for powdery mildew as the season warms.

common_name: Blue Dune Lyme Grass (Steel-Blue European Dune Grass)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained, even sandy soil; give it room or a barrier since it spreads by rhizomes and resents staying wet.

directions: Blue Dune Lyme Grass carries intensely steel-blue, coarse blades on a cool-season clump that spreads by rhizomes, originally selected for stabilizing coastal dunes in Britain and Western Europe. It wants full sun and sharply drained, on-the-dry-side soil, since it is notably sensitive to overwatering and will decline in heavy, wet ground. Straw-colored seed heads appear in late spring, and cutting the whole clump back afterward encourages fresh, cleanly colored blue foliage through autumn. Because it spreads steadily, it earns its keep best on a slope, bank, or sandy area needing erosion control rather than in a tightly mixed border.

subcategory: warm-season ornamental grass, often grown as an annual

planting.note: Set out plants in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, in well-drained soil or containers; north of its hardy range grow it as a warm-season annual.

directions: Savannah Ruby Grass is a named selection of the southern African native ruby grass, grown for its showy midsummer plumes, which open deep pink-burgundy and shift through shimmering, iridescent shades of pink that hold their color for weeks, set against light bluish-green foliage. It is very drought tolerant once established and thrives in full sun with sharp drainage, making it well suited to containers and hot, dry sites. Hardy only to about zone 8, it is commonly grown as a warm-season annual bedding or container plant farther north, prized for its long bloom display and soft, touchable seed heads. Avoid rich, consistently wet soil, which encourages lax growth at the expense of flowering.

common_name: Dreamer Double Early Tulip (Ballerina-Pink Peony-Flowered Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep about six weeks before the ground freezes, in compost-enriched soil that drains well.

directions: Dreamer belongs to the early double class, opening fully packed, peony-like blooms that start out a soft ballerina pink brushed with apricot-gold before fading to a muted champagne tone as they age. Because it flowers low and early, it suits the front of a border, mass plantings, or containers where its long-lasting double form can be appreciated up close. Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil and let the foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom so the bulb can recharge for the following spring. In mild-winter regions chill bulbs before planting, and apply a repellent or wire basket if moles or gophers are a problem.

common_name: Double Surprise Tulip (White and Magenta Double Late Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall, about six weeks before the ground freezes, in compost-enriched well-drained soil.

directions: A double late tulip, Double Surprise carries large 3-4 inch blooms with bright white centers feathered and flushed in deep magenta, giving a layered, peony-like flower that opens later in the season than the double earlies. Plant the bulbs deeply in fall so they anchor well against wind and frost heave, and work compost into the planting hole to feed the developing root system. After bloom, resist the urge to cut back the leaves and instead let them brown naturally, since that foliage is what rebuilds the bulb for next year's flowers. The sturdy stems and heavy flower heads make excellent cut flowers but also benefit from a somewhat sheltered spot to avoid flopping in wind or rain.

common_name: Tiny Dancer Dwarf Globeflower (Mat-Forming Blue-Flowered Globularia)

planting.note: Tuck plugs into lean, sharply drained soil in a crevice garden, rock garden, or paver gap rather than enriched garden soil.

directions: This dwarf globularia forms a tight, nearly flat evergreen mat only an inch or two tall, studded in late spring with small round true-blue flower puffs that read like tiny disco balls scattered across the foliage. It is built for lean, mineral soils rather than rich garden beds, so site it on a berm, in a crevice garden, or between stepping stones where drainage is sharp and competition from larger plants is minimal. Full sun suits it in most climates, though afternoon shade helps in the hottest regions, and established plants need very little supplemental water. Because the spreading mat stays so low and dense, it works well as a durable edging or infill plant for rock gardens and xeric borders.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Blueberry Lemonade pairs the familiar late-summer haze of purple-blue bluebeard flowers with bright chartreuse foliage, a color combination that keeps the shrub visually interesting for months before the fuzzy flower clusters even open. Like other caryopteris, it blooms on new wood and often dies back partway or fully to the ground in cold winters, so treat it as a woody-based perennial rather than a permanent shrub skeleton. It thrives in lean to average soil with excellent drainage and shrugs off heat and drought once established, making it a good fit for waterwise borders. Cut the whole plant back hard in early spring before new growth starts to keep it compact, floriferous, and well-shaped for the coming season.

common_name: Nature's Beauty Grape Hyacinth (Seafoam-Blue Fading Muscari)

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3-4 inches deep and close together in fall for the fullest effect; they naturalize and multiply over time.

directions: Nature's Beauty offers an unusual color shift among grape hyacinths, opening in a light, slightly seafoam-tinted blue and fading gradually to cream as the tiny bell-shaped florets age up the spike, so a single clump shows two tones at once in peak bloom. Plant the small bulbs in generous drifts in fall, since grape hyacinths look best massed rather than scattered as single specimens, and they are small enough to tuck between larger perennials or naturalize in a lawn edge. Once established in well-drained soil they need little care, returning and slowly multiplying into denser clumps each year with no digging or dividing required. Let the grassy foliage fade on its own after bloom, which also helps the planting go unnoticed once flowering finishes for the season.

common_name: Creme de Cassis Dahlia (Lilac-Pink and Plum-Wine Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 1-2 inches deep after soil has warmed past 55F, once spring frost danger has passed.

directions: Creme de Cassis is a decorative dahlia whose petals layer dusty lilac-pink on the face and deep plum-wine on the reverse, creating a soft watercolor blending effect as the large blooms open and the two tones show through together. Plant tubers after the soil has warmed in spring, stake or site plants against a wall or fence for wind protection, since the big flowers on tall stems can catch wind, and keep soil evenly moist with regular feeding through the growing season. Flowers build through midsummer and continue steadily until frost, making this a strong choice for cutting gardens where hummingbirds and butterflies are also drawn to the blooms. In regions colder than zone 8, lift the tubers after the first hard frost blackens the foliage and store them dry and cool over winter for replanting the following spring.

planting.note: Plant corms about 8 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.

directions: Tina belongs to the dwarf Glamini gladiolus group, bred for a shorter, garden-friendly stature compared with tall exhibition gladiolus, with lavender-mauve florets deepening to a dramatic wine-purple throat at the center of each flower. Blooms open in sequence starting at the bottom of the spike and working upward over several days, which extends the display on each stem well beyond a single bloom flush. Plant corms deeply in full sun once soil has warmed in spring, and keep the planting evenly watered through the growing season since gladiolus perform poorly under drought stress. In cold climates dig and store corms after fall frost kills the foliage, or simply treat the planting as a one-season annual display.

common_name: Bordeaux Anemone (Wine-Red De Caen Poppy Anemone)

planting.note: Soak corms about 2 hours in lukewarm water before planting 3 inches deep in compost-enriched, well-drained soil.

directions: Bordeaux is a De Caen-type poppy anemone with single, satiny wine-red to burgundy petals surrounding a near-black central boss of stamens, a dramatic color pairing on a plant that stays low and tidy at under a foot tall. Soaking the knobby little corms in lukewarm water for a couple of hours before planting speeds rehydration and improves sprouting odds compared with planting them bone dry. Plant in compost-enriched, well-drained soil in full sun or morning sun with afternoon shade, and expect bloom within a couple of months of planting, which makes it useful for filling gaps in spring and early summer beds or for cutting. In regions colder than zone 8 treat the corms as a seasonal planting, or lift and store them after foliage fades for replanting again the following year.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in full sun after frost danger passes, and grow in a container to move under cover where winters dip below the mid-20s F.

directions: Fukumoto is a Japanese-bred sport of the standard navel orange, prized for reaching legal maturity three to four weeks ahead of Washington navel while staying a noticeably smaller, more compact tree. Grow it in full sun with regular irrigation and good drainage, and expect a deep reddish-orange rind on fruit harvested from mid-fall into early winter. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree planted in-ground in zone 9-11 or container-grown further north will set a full crop without a second variety.

common_name: GE Neri Fig (Sweet Italian Tennis-Ball Fig)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun with excellent drainage; in zone 7-8 give it a sheltered microclimate or grow in a container to overwinter indoors.

directions: GE Neri is a sweet Italian fig selection that produces unusually large, tennis-ball-sized fruit on a self-fertile, thornless shrub. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but dislikes soggy soil, so plant it in full sun on a well-drained site or raised bed. Because it is only rated hardy to about zone 8, gardeners in zone 7 should grow it in a large container and move it to shelter for winter.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or very early spring in rich, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates; this cross shows unusually good heat tolerance for a gooseberry.

directions: Glenndale crosses American and European gooseberry parentage to combine mildew immunity with good fruit flavor, ripening early to a purple-red color on a thorny, 3-6 foot deciduous shrub. Give it partial shade in warm climates and full sun in cooler ones, in fertile soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. It is self-fertile, so a single bush will produce a full crop, and its disease resistance makes it a lower-maintenance choice than many gooseberry cultivars.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and site a second genetically distinct chestnut nearby to ensure good pollination.

directions: Improved Chinese Chestnut is a named selection of the blight-resistant Chinese chestnut, grown as a broad, spreading 30-40 foot shade-and-nut tree for home orchards. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and expect large, glossy, sweet nuts that drop naturally in early to mid-fall once the burs split open. It benefits from cross-pollination with a second, unrelated chestnut tree planted nearby, and tolerates lighter or less fertile soils better than most other nut trees once established.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or potted trees in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; no second tree is needed since it is self-fertile.

directions: Calliope combines the cold hardiness of the American persimmon with the rich flavor of Asian kaki types, producing orange fruit that ranges from non-astringent to lightly astringent depending on how ripe it is picked. It grows into a 15-20 foot self-fertile tree with glossy green summer foliage that turns yellow and orange in fall, and the fruit often hangs on the bare branches well after leaf drop. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil, where it needs no spray program and tolerates both heat and moderate drought once established.

common_name: Smith's Best Persimmon (Dwarf Asian Persimmon, Giboshi)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; its naturally dwarf, compact habit makes it a good choice for small yards or containers.

directions: Smith's Best, also sold as Giboshi, is a naturally dwarf Asian persimmon selected from J. Russell Smith's historic homestead planting in Front Royal, Virginia. Its compact, self-fertile tree produces top-shaped fruit early in the persimmon season, best eaten once fully soft. Give it full sun and well-drained soil; its small stature makes it one of the easier Asian persimmons to fit into a limited-space garden or large container, and it needs no spray to stay healthy.

common_name: Veritage Grape (Cold-Hardy Northern Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines on a trellis in full sun in spring; train and prune to manage its vigorous 15-20 foot growth.

directions: Veritage is a cold-hardy red wine grape bred by Minnesota breeder Tom Plocher for northern vineyards, valued for its winter hardiness, spring frost resistance, and resistance to powdery and downy mildew. The vigorous vines need a sturdy trellis and full sun, and produce dark blue-black grapes in mid-season with balanced acidity suited to wines with notes of raspberry, plum, and chocolate. It is self-fertile and well suited to regions too cold for traditional European wine grapes.

subcategory: long-blooming full-sun border perennial (Magic Show series)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil and remove spent spikes to encourage the next wave of flower wands.

directions: Part of a compact speedwell series bred for a tidy, floriferous habit, this selection sends up dense violet-purple flower spikes that open sequentially from base to tip starting in midsummer. The deep green foliage stays attractive and disease-free through the season, giving the plant a neat presence even between bloom cycles. It performs best in full sun with average, well-drained soil and needs little more than occasional deadheading to keep flowering into fall. Its low-maintenance habit and pollinator appeal make it a dependable mid-border filler.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into average, well-drained soil where the spreading mound can be used as a groundcover between taller perennials.

directions: This hardy cranesbill forms a low, spreading mound of finely cut foliage topped with cup-shaped, dark-veined pink-purple flowers from late spring through late summer. Foliage shifts from green to burgundy in autumn, adding a second season of interest after bloom. It adapts to both full sun and half-day shade and tolerates a wide range of temperatures, making it a forgiving choice for groundcover, edging, or container use. Shearing the mound back after the first flush encourages fresh growth and a second round of bloom.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring into consistently moist soil in a shaded or woodland setting where the compact rosettes won't dry out.

directions: This double-flowered primrose produces fragrant white blooms edged in blue-violet with a picotee margin and a bright yellow eye, held just above a low rosette of crinkled leaves. It flowers from early to late spring and is sized for the front of a shaded or partly sunny border, woodland garden, or container. Keep the soil consistently moist, since primroses are shallow-rooted and dry out quickly in sun or wind. Its compact habit and long bloom window make it a good companion for later-emerging hostas and ferns in a mixed shade bed.

planting.note: Plant in spring into average to clay soil in full sun; established plants shrug off summer drought and need little supplemental water.

directions: This coneflower selection carries pink ray petals tipped in crisp white, giving each daisy-form bloom a manicured, two-tone look around a prominent central cone. It flowers from early summer through mid-fall, drawing butterflies, bees, and seed-eating songbirds, and holds up well as a cut flower. Like other coneflowers it tolerates heat, drought, humidity, and poor soil once rooted in, needing only occasional water during establishment. Leave spent flower heads standing into winter to feed birds and let the clump self-sow lightly at the garden's edge.

planting.note: Plant after last frost into sandy, sharply drained soil, since penstemon crowns are prone to rot in heavy or wet winter ground.

directions: This compact beardtongue sends up spikes of tubular, bell-shaped lilac flowers from early summer into mid-fall, attracting bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds over a long season. It prefers lean, sandy, fast-draining soil and full sun, performing best where winter moisture doesn't pool around the crown. Established plants tolerate drought well and make a tidy, floriferous addition to a sunny border or gravel garden. Cutting spent spikes back encourages rebloom and keeps the compact habit from flopping open.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in spring in heavy, humus-rich, slightly acid soil kept constantly moist, such as a pond margin or rain garden.

directions: Among the largest-flowered Japanese irises, this selection opens ruffled, upward-facing blooms with violet-blue outer falls, dark purple standards, and a bright yellow signal patch, resembling butterflies perched above the strap-like foliage. It blooms from early to late summer and needs consistently wet, slightly acidic, organically rich soil to perform well, making it a natural fit for pond edges, stream banks, or rain gardens. Unlike bearded irises, it will not tolerate dry summer soil and should never be allowed to sit in alkaline or lime-heavy ground. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
